title: Acclimation of Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 to alkaline pH under ambient air
projectDescription: Cyanobacteria are able to grow at a wide pH range and for many strains their growth is enhanced in alkaline environment. In this study, we investigated the proteomic response of the cyanobacterium of Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 to alkaline pH. The proteomes of Synechocystis grown in BG-11 medium buffered at pH 7.5, pH 8.2 and pH 9.2 were analysed by a mass spectrometry-based (LC-MS/MS) data-dependent acquisition (DDA) method. Total proteins (membrane and soluble) from unfractionated Synechocystis cell lysates were investigated.
sampleProcessingProtocol: A glucose-tolerant wild-type strain of Synechocystis was utilized for this study. Cells were cultivated at 30°C in an atmospheric CO2 concentration of 427 ppm CO₂ under continuous illumination of 50 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ provided by white LED lights. The cultures, each consisting of 30 mL in 100 mL Erlenmeyer flasks, were agitated at 120 rpm. All experimental cultures were grown in AlgaeTron AG230 growth chambers (PSI Instruments) equipped with cool-white LEDs. The BG-11 medium was buffered using 20 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 20 mM TES-KOH (pH 8.2), or 20 mM CHES (pH 9.2), depending on the experimental pH conditions. Pre-experimental cultures were grown for 4 days in 30 mL of BG-11 medium buffered for the respective pH regimes. Experimental cultures were inoculated at an OD₇₅₀ of 0.1 in 30 mL of BG-11 medium supplemented with the corresponding buffer. Cultures were grown until reaching an OD₇₅₀ of approximately 0.9. Cells were harvested by centrifugation at 8,000 × g for 10 minutes at 4°C and washed twice with 50 mM TES-KOH buffer (pH 8.0). The cell pellet was resuspended in a protein extraction buffer containing 0.1% (w/v) RapiGest SF (Waters Corporation) in 8 M urea solubilized in 0.1 M Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), supplemented with 200 µM PMSF and an equal volume of acid-washed glass beads (150-212 µm, Sigma). Cells were lysed using a Bullet Blender homogenizer (Next Advance) with six cycles of 45 seconds of shaking, interspersed with 3-minute incubations on ice. Unbroken cells and glass beads were removed by centrifugation at 1,000 × g for 5 minutes and subsequently at 12,000 × g for 20 minutes at room temperature. Protein concentration was determined using the Bradford method (Bio-Rad). Proteins were reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol (DTT, Sigma), alkylated with 10 mM iodoacetamide (IAA, Sigma), and precipitated overnight at -20°C with a 1:5 (v/v) mixture of 50% acetone and 50% ethanol. The pellet was centrifuged at 16,500 × g at 4°C for 30 minutes and solubilized by trypsin digestion (1:100 trypsin:protein ratio) in 50 mM Tris-HCl and 5% (v/v) acetonitrile (ACN) buffer for 5 hours at 37°C with shaking. Digestion was continued for an additional 16 hours following a second addition of trypsin. The digestion was halted by adding formic acid (FA) to a final concentration of 0.5-1% (v/v), lowering the pH below 2. The mixture was incubated for 30 minutes at 37°C at 500 rpm, and the water-immiscible RapiGest SF degradation products were removed by centrifugation. Peptides were desalted using solid-phase extraction (SPE) with a Wet Sep-Pak 100 mg C18 96-well plate according to the manufacturer's protocol. The eluted peptide samples were vacuum-dried and solubilized in 0.1% (v/v) FA, then stored at -80°C prior to MS analysis. A set of iRT peptides (Biognosys) was added to the sample before LC-MS injection.
dataProcessingProtocol: Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-ESI-MS/MS) analyses were conducted using a nanoflow HPLC system (Easy-nLC1200, Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to a Q Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany) equipped with a nano-electrospray ionization source. Peptides equivalent to 400 ng from four biological replicates per condition were loaded in a randomized order onto the nLC column. An in-house packed 40 cm, 75 µm ID capillary column with 1.9 µm Reprosil-Pur C18 beads (Dr. Maisch) was used, with the column temperature maintained at 60°C. The mobile phase consisted of water with 0.1% formic acid (solvent A) or acetonitrile/water (80:20 v/v) with 0.1% formic acid (solvent B). Peptides were separated by a stepped 110 min gradient (70 min 5–26% B, 30 min 26–49% B, 5 min 49–100% B and 5 min 100% B). MS data were acquired using Thermo Xcalibur 3.1 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Protein identification and label-free data-dependent acquisition (DDA) involved an Orbitrap MS survey scan with a mass range of 300-1800 m/z, followed by HCD fragmentation for the 10 most intense peptide ions with a charge ≥ 2. Spectra were detected with resolutions of 120,000 and 15,000 (at m/z 200) for full scan and fragment ions, respectively, using a normalized collision energy of 27%. The automatic gain control (AGC) was set to 3e6 and 1e5 ions, with maximum ion injection times of 100 ms and 250 ms for MS and MS/MS scans, respectively. Data files were searched against the Synechocystis database from Cyanobase (3672 entries, October 23, 2012) using Proteome Discoverer 2.5 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific) connected to an in-house server running the Mascot 2.6.1 algorithm (Matrix Science). The precursor mass tolerance was set to ±10 ppm, and the fragment ion mass tolerance was ±0.02 Da. Two missed cleavages were allowed, and decoy searches were performed. Spectrum identifications were validated using the Percolator algorithm with a relaxed false discovery rate of 0.05.
